title: IP Integration Challenges Evolve
gist: IP integration has grown from tens of blocks to thousands of configurable, often encrypted IPs, with the worst bugs arising between blocks from ambiguous specs, unwritten hardware-software assumptions, power-domain interactions and, increasingly, chiplets that turn IP integration into multi-vendor supply-chain integration; tooling for formal verification, telemetry IP and lifecycle/version management is evolving to keep the relative pain constant.

themes.theme: Scale and nature of IP integration complexity

insights.claim: The Virtual Socket Interface Alliance (VSIA), formed in 1996 to standardize how third-party IP was built, verified and delivered, dissolved in 2008, yet the IP integration problem continues to evolve eighteen years later.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: IP integration remains an unsolved, persistent pain point sustaining EDA/IP-management demand.
insights.locator: The creation of the Virtual Socket Interface Alliance

insights.claim: Keysight EDA's Pedro Pires says designs that had tens of IP blocks ten years ago now sit within companies holding thousands of IPs and dozens of versions of the same IP, each far more configurable, making ad hoc management very difficult.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Explosive IP counts drive demand for IP lifecycle/data-management tools.
insights.quote: Today, a company may have thousands of IPs, dozens of different versions of the same IP, and you want to make sense of all of this.
insights.locator: “Ten years ago, a design may have had tens

insights.claim: IC Manage CEO Dean Drako argues chip complexity is not proportional to size, since a 32-core CPU is 32 copies and a giant cache is one cell repeated 100 million times.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Transistor count is a poor proxy for design/verification effort and EDA spend.
insights.quote: The complexity is not always proportional to the size of the chip.
insights.locator: While design size has steadily increased

insights.claim: Axiomise's Ashish Darbari frames integration complexity as the number of assumptions a block makes about its environment: a UART needs a clock, reset and register interface, while a coherent cache, CHI home node or NoC carries hundreds of assumptions (ordering rules, credit contracts, outstanding-transaction limits, power sequencing, address maps, security attributes).
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Interconnect and coherency IP carry disproportionate integration risk and verification value.
insights.quote: What matters is how many assumptions a block makes about the world around it, and that number climbs much faster than size.
insights.locator: What matters is how many assumptions

insights.claim: Darbari says the nastiest failures occur between blocks (message-dependent deadlock, leaking credits, corrupted reorder buffers, ordering rules broken across bridges) where each block passes its own verification but the system hangs because two teams read a protocol rule differently.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: System-level/formal verification addressing cross-IP semantics is a growing tool market.
insights.quote: The nastiest failures are almost never inside a single block
insights.locator: This puts a lot of stress on verification.

insights.claim: Synopsys' Madhumita Sanyal lists rising cross-IP issues spanning address mapping, interrupts, coherency, QoS, security, DVFS, software/OS interaction and, for die-to-die IP, interoperability, known-good-die, signal/power integrity, thermal coupling and telemetry.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Breadth of cross-IP concerns expands the scope of integration and verification tooling.
insights.locator: Over time, the number of cross-IP issues

themes.theme: Bad specifications as the root cause

insights.claim: Semantic issues, many stemming from incomplete or bad IP specifications, cause the most integration problems, beyond simply ensuring blocks are properly connected.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Spec-capture and executable-specification tools address the highest-cost bug class.
insights.locator: Key Takeaways:

insights.claim: Darbari says differing interpretations of intended system behavior exist from day one because nobody wrote them down in a shared form, and they surface about two years later, often in post-silicon debug when they are most expensive to fix.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Late-discovered spec bugs drive costly respins, motivating shift-left formal methods.
insights.quote: They just surface two years later, often in post-silicon debug, when they are most expensive to fix.
insights.locator: The problem is often discovered

insights.claim: Darbari notes large IP increasingly arrives encrypted, leaving integrators reliant on documentation, which in his experience is often where the bug is.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Encrypted IP raises integration risk and the value of black-box/formal verification.
insights.quote: You’re left with the documentation, and in my experience that is often where the bug is.
insights.locator: Verification: With IP, and even more so

insights.claim: IP is increasingly shipped as configurable generators; vendors verify some configurations but customers often tape out a different one, and with more than a handful of parameters it is easy to hit an untested combination.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Configuration-space explosion creates hidden tape-out risk and demand for config-aware verification.
insights.quote: The vendor verified some set of configurations, but you are probably taping out a different one.
insights.locator: Verification: With IP, and even more so

insights.claim: Synopsys' Sanyal says identifying legal subsets of IP functionality to verify is an architecture task that cannot be generically automated, though AI models are now used by Synopsys and customers to reach corner cases faster.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: AI-assisted verification is entering production use at major EDA vendors.
insights.locator: The good news should be that not every

insights.claim: Sanyal says even a PHY has significant software content (boot firmware, continuously updated calibration firmware, drivers tied to OS interrupts, DMA, BIOS, hypervisor and IOMMU dependencies).
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Rising software content in IP increases cross-domain integration and verification effort.
insights.quote: Even something as simple as a PHY has a significant software content,
insights.locator: Software complexity: While some software

insights.claim: Darbari says UCIe 3.0 standardizes early firmware download, but hardware is often only correct under unwritten software assumptions (e.g., register programming order) that RTL verification never checks.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Standards alone don't close HW/SW correctness gaps; co-verification tools have room to grow.
insights.quote: Those rules are rarely written down, and RTL verification on its own never checks them.
insights.locator: These issues are problematic enough

insights.claim: Darbari warns a field firmware update can change silicon behavior after sign-off, with conflicts over interrupts, power states, DMA buffers and security attributes surfacing at bring-up when the first real driver runs.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Post-signoff firmware changes create ongoing reliability and security risk.
insights.quote: A firmware update in the field can change how silicon behaves after it was signed off,
insights.locator: Hardware and software ship and update

insights.claim: Pires says the link between specific hardware and software versions often lives in Excel spreadsheets, which is messy and error-prone, creating a need for persistent, traceable system bill-of-materials management.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Highlights a tooling gap for unified HW/SW configuration management.
insights.quote: this is a link that exists often in Excel spreadsheets, which is messy and error-prone.
insights.locator: Hardware and software generally use different

insights.claim: Drako says AI may speed IP lifecycles, but companies still need data and systems to track what was taped out, built, and which IP was used where.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: AI adoption increases rather than removes the need for IP lifecycle management infrastructure.
insights.locator: Very few things are perfect

themes.theme: Power, thermal and analog as integration drivers

insights.claim: Darbari says power management has become a functional feature and a major source of functional bugs, e.g., a block dropping a transaction when a neighbor powers down mid-transfer, which simulation rarely catches but formal methods can.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Power-domain complexity boosts demand for formal verification tools.
insights.quote: Power management has become a functional feature, and a major source of functional bugs,
insights.locator: Power and thermal: Controlling power

insights.claim: Agile Analog's Chris Morrison says with power and thermal driving SoC limits, analog IP must actively manage chips via embedded PVT sensors, timing monitors, droop and glitch detectors feeding real-time telemetry to power-management units.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Growing market for on-chip sensing/telemetry analog IP.
insights.quote: analog IP can’t just sit there passively anymore,
insights.locator: When power is consumed it generates heat

insights.claim: Pires says AI automation for RF and analog design is hampered by scarce, narrow and often proprietary training data.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Analog/RF design may lag in AI-driven EDA productivity gains.
insights.locator: Analog content: Analog content has always

insights.claim: Morrison says customers increasingly want complete analog subsystems with digital wrappers and SystemVerilog real-number models so SoC teams can run full-chip verification without slow SPICE simulation.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Shift toward subsystem-level analog IP offerings raises vendor value capture.

themes.theme: Chiplets turn IP integration into supply-chain integration

insights.claim: Synopsys' Frank Schirrmeister says chiplets move integration from the SoC boundary to the package boundary, turning IP integration into supply-chain integration across different companies, nodes and foundries with differing verification methodologies.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Chiplet adoption creates multi-vendor integration risk and demand for cross-company verification flows.
insights.quote: Now it turns IP integration into supply chain integration.
insights.locator: Chiplets: Chiplets can be viewed

insights.claim: Darbari says UCIe handles physical and link layers well and cross-vendor interoperability is being demonstrated, but address maps, coherency models and software remain semantic questions standards leave open, with chiplets becoming small systems with their own management firmware.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: A working UCIe link does not guarantee an open chiplet marketplace; semantic integration remains a barrier.
insights.quote: But a working link doesn’t make a working system.
insights.locator: None of the integration issues go away.

insights.claim: Pires says chiplets bring multi-physics concerns requiring much more data per IP, such as power intent traveling with the IP as an additional artifact.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Metadata management for chiplets is an expanding EDA niche.
insights.locator: Chiplets need even more information

insights.claim: Licensing, geopolitical restrictions and export controls are cited as additional pressures complicating IP integration.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Export controls add a compliance dimension to IP selection and tracking.
insights.locator: Many areas add to the integration pressures

insights.claim: Pires argues IP management mechanisms evolve alongside the problem, so in relative terms the pain stays constant even as the underlying problem grows.
insights.speaker: Brian Bailey
insights.so_what: Suggests steady, growing EDA investment rather than a crisis-driven inflection.
insights.quote: In relative terms, the pain remains constant, but the problem underlying it is a bigger one.
